title: Make Work Pay: Threshold for triggering collective redundancy obligations (consultation)
date_evidence:
Launch date: 26 February 2026
Closing Date: 21 May 2026
key_claim: The Employment Rights Act 2025 adds an organisation-wide trigger for collective redundancy consultation alongside the existing 20-at-one-establishment test, because dispersed redundancies currently escape consultation entirely; the provisions are expected in force in 2027.
frame_summary: The consultation argues that the establishment-based trigger produces arbitrary outcomes because entitlement depends on how redundancies happen to be distributed across sites, and that an organisation-wide threshold is needed to capture large dispersed programmes without leaving the biggest employers permanently in consultation.
verbatim_quote: This means an employer can make large numbers of employees redundant without being required to undertake any collective consultation where redundancies are dispersed across an organisation.
verbatim_list: In the worst cases this has led to thousands of employees not being able to benefit from collective consultation.

This can also lead to unfairness among employees, as it means that whether an employee will be entitled to collective consultation (or a protective award for non-compliance), will depend on how redundancies are distributed across establishments.
These provisions of the Employment Rights Act 2025 are expected to be brought into force in 2027.
The power does not allow the threshold to be set at a number lower than 20.

title: Employment Rights Act 2025
key_claim: From 6 April 2026 the maximum protective award for failure to consult in collective redundancy is 180 days' pay, and from 2027 employers must consider the total number of redundancies across the whole organisation rather than individual workplaces.
frame_summary: Acas presents the Act as a sequenced set of employer obligations landing between 2026 and 2027, with the collective-redundancy changes framed as an operational compliance timetable employers should prepare for now.
verbatim_quote: From 6 April 2026, the maximum 'protective award' for failure to consult in collective redundancy is 180 days' pay. Before 6 April 2026, it was 90 days' pay.
verbatim_list: employers will need to consider the total number of redundancies across their whole organisation, not just individual workplaces – currently, collective redundancy rules only apply to individual workplaces

title: The OECD AI exposure measure: Mapping the OECD AI Capability Indicators to occupations
key_claim: AI capability is closest to occupations built on routine information processing, administrative work and codifiable tasks, and furthest from those requiring contextual judgement and responsibility.
frame_summary: The paper argues that AI exposure should be measured as a capability gap between what AI systems can do and what occupations require, and that exposure is multidimensional rather than a single displacement score, with actual impact dependent on adoption, regulation and organisational choice.
verbatim_quote: current AI capabilities are closest to occupations involving routine information processing, administrative work and codifiable tasks, and furthest from occupations requiring contextual judgement, interpersonal understanding, complex decision making and responsibility
notes: Supplies the occupational shape of exposure that explains why AI-driven reductions land thinly across many sites. Quote read from the live page during WebFetch on 2026-08-01; automated provenance re-fetch returns 403 inside the Cowork sandbox (documented tooling limit).

title: OECD Employment Outlook 2026: Geographic Disparities in Jobs and Incomes
key_claim: Local labour markets are being reshaped by trade and technology shocks including artificial intelligence, and gaps in employment and incomes across regions are large and persistent.
frame_summary: The Outlook argues that where a worker lives increasingly determines labour-market outcomes, so technology shocks land unevenly across regions and mobility alone will not close the resulting gaps.

title: Workplace transformation: Employer obligations in EU AI-driven restructuring scenarios, with examples from France and Germany
date_evidence:
Jul 14 2026

The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) and its increasing use in companies is leading to profound changes in the workplace.
key_claim: German works-council co-determination under Section 87(1)(6) BetrVG is triggered by virtually any AI use capable of recording or evaluating employee behaviour, and the process can take from a few weeks to several months before a system may be introduced.
frame_summary: The authors argue that AI deployment and AI-driven staff reductions in the EU are governed by information and consultation rights that bite before implementation, so employers should treat consultation design and skills-based social plans as part of the transformation plan rather than a downstream formality.
verbatim_quote: German labour courts interpret this right of co-determination very broadly, with the result that virtually any use of AI falls under this provision and is subject to co-determination, regardless of whether the employer actually intends to monitor performance and behaviour of the employee.
verbatim_list: Companies may only introduce AI systems once the entire co-determination procedure has been completed. This process can take from a few weeks to several months.
In some jurisdictions, failure to comply with mandatory information and consultation procedures where these are required gives rise to criminal liability

title: Give workers more say over AI, UK thinktank IPPR urges
key_claim: A TUC-backed IPPR report recommends a statutory duty on employers to consult staff on AI adoption, with cited survey data showing 21% of workers say AI has worsened their working life against 20% who say it has improved it.
frame_summary: The report is framed as an argument about power rather than technology: whether AI augments, degrades or displaces work depends on who shapes adoption, so consultation rights are the lever being proposed.
verbatim_quote: Survey data cited shows 21% of workers say AI has worsened their working life against 20% who say it has improved it, with 4% believing they have already lost a job to the technology.
verbatim_list: It recommends a statutory duty on employers to consult staff on AI adoption, plus a “worker support levy” funding a portable wallet of benefits such as training and union membership.
notes: Trade-press coverage of the IPPR/TUC report, used for the direction of policy pressure rather than as a primary source for the underlying survey.
